body.statement:
On balanced squares \(n_B=n_S=n\) at \(R=4\), define
\[
\ell(n)=\min\{d\in\mathbb Z:d\ge2,\ d\mid n\}.
\]
For every integer \(n\ge3\), every proper positive divisor \(k\mid n\) is eligible in the published equal-square block comparator, whereas \(k=n\) is ineligible. Consequently, the largest eligible block size is \(n/\ell(n)\), and
\[
\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)=\frac{2n^2}{\ell(n)},
\qquad
\Phi_{n,n}(4)=2(n-1)^2+2.
\]
Thus the exact gain of the covering paired-rectangle class over the published equal-square subclass and their exact retention ratio are
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(4)-\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)
=2(n-1)^2+2-\frac{2n^2}{\ell(n)}
\]
and
\[
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}
=\ell(n)\left(1-\frac{2}{n}+\frac{2}{n^2}\right).
\]
In particular,
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(4)-\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)\ge(n-2)^2>0
\]
and
\[
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}
\ge2-\frac4n+\frac4{n^2},
\]
with equality in either lower bound if and only if \(n\) is even. The even integers therefore form the sharp factor-two asymptotic lower envelope, and
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}=2.
\]
If \(n\) is prime, then
\[
\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)=2n,
\qquad
\Phi_{n,n}(4)-\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)=2(n-1)(n-2),
\qquad
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}=n-2+\frac2n,
\]
so prime balanced sizes exhibit linear-scale ratio separation.
body.justification: The exact least-divisor formula shows that the catalog is not merely a notational enlargement of the published equal-square family: unequal covering rectangles strictly improve focal retention for every balanced size \(n\ge3\), even sizes give the sharp factor-two asymptotic lower envelope, and prime sizes give ratio \(n-2+2/n\).
body.gap: The published equal-square calculation optimizes only over equal block sizes and does not identify that its support-four optimum is \(2n^2/\ell(n)\), nor the resulting exact separation from the covering paired-rectangle frontier.
body.consumer: Researchers using the published equal-block rule can compute its exact support-four benchmark from the least nontrivial divisor of the balanced population size and quantify the precise focal-size gain from allowing unequal covering rectangles.
body.proof_tex:
Fix an integer \(n\ge3\). The set
\[
\{d\in\mathbb Z:d\ge2,\ d\mid n\}
\]
is nonempty because it contains \(n\), and it is finite because each of its elements lies between \(2\) and \(n\). Hence its minimum \(\ell(n)\) is well defined.

Let \(k\) be a positive divisor of \(n\), and put \(r=n/k\). Then \(r\) is a positive integer. By \(\textnormal{def:equal-square-comparator}\), the block size \(k\) is eligible at \(R=4\) exactly when
\[
\binom{2n/k}{n/k}=\binom{2r}{r}\ge4,
\]
and its retained focal count is \(2nk\). If \(k=n\), then \(r=1\), and
\[
\binom{2r}{r}=\binom21=2<4,
\]
so \(k=n\) is ineligible.

Suppose instead that \(k\) is a proper divisor of \(n\). Because \(k\) and \(n\) are positive and \(k<n\), the integer \(r=n/k\) satisfies \(r\ge2\). Direct calculation gives
\[
\binom42=6.
\]
Moreover, for every positive integer \(s\), positivity of the factorials permits division and yields
\[
\frac{\binom{2(s+1)}{s+1}}{\binom{2s}{s}}
=\frac{(2s+2)(2s+1)}{(s+1)^2}
=\frac{2(2s+1)}{s+1}>1,
\]
where the last inequality follows from \(2(2s+1)-(s+1)=3s+1>0\). Induction from \(s=2\) therefore gives
\[
\binom{2r}{r}\ge\binom42=6\ge4.
\]
Thus every proper divisor \(k\mid n\) is eligible. We have proved that the eligible block sizes at \(R=4\) are exactly the proper positive divisors of \(n\).

The score \(2nk\) is strictly increasing in \(k\) because \(2n>0\). For a proper divisor \(k\), the co-divisor \(d=n/k\) is a divisor of \(n\) satisfying \(d\ge2\), and conversely every such \(d\) gives the proper divisor \(k=n/d\). Since division of the positive number \(n\) is order reversing on positive denominators, the largest eligible \(k\) corresponds to the smallest such \(d\), namely \(d=\ell(n)\). Hence \(\textnormal{def:equal-square-comparator}\) gives the exact published-subclass optimum
\[
\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)
=2n\frac{n}{\ell(n)}
=\frac{2n^2}{\ell(n)}.
\]
In particular this quantity is positive, so every later division by it is valid.

The hypotheses of the already established \(\textnormal{prop:r4-reduction}\) hold because \(n_B=n_S=n\ge3\). That proposition gives the exact covering paired-rectangle frontier
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(4)=2(n-1)^2+2.
\]
Subtracting the preceding exact comparator formula proves
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(4)-\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)
=2(n-1)^2+2-\frac{2n^2}{\ell(n)}.
\]
Likewise, positivity of \(2n^2/\ell(n)\) permits division, and elementary algebra gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}
&=\frac{2(n-1)^2+2}{2n^2/\ell(n)}\\
&=\ell(n)\frac{(n-1)^2+1}{n^2}\\
&=\ell(n)\left(1-\frac2n+\frac{2}{n^2}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]

By definition \(\ell(n)\ge2\), so
\[
\frac{2n^2}{\ell(n)}\le n^2.
\]
Substitution in the exact gap gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Phi_{n,n}(4)-\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)
&\ge2(n-1)^2+2-n^2\\
&=(n-2)^2>0,
\end{aligned}
\]
where strict positivity uses \(n\ge3\). The factor
\[
1-\frac2n+\frac{2}{n^2}=\frac{(n-1)^2+1}{n^2}
\]
is positive. Multiplying \(\ell(n)\ge2\) by this factor therefore gives
\[
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}
\ge2-\frac4n+\frac4{n^2}.
\]
Equality in either lower bound holds exactly when \(2n^2/\ell(n)=n^2\), equivalently when \(\ell(n)=2\). By the definition of \(\ell(n)\), the equality \(\ell(n)=2\) holds exactly when \(2\mid n\), that is, exactly when \(n\) is even.

The ratio lower bound converges to \(2\) as \(n\to\infty\), hence
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}\ge2.
\]
For every even \(n\), the equality case just proved gives
\[
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}
=2-\frac4n+\frac4{n^2}\longrightarrow2
\]
along the infinite sequence of even integers. The full limit inferior is therefore at most \(2\), and the two inequalities prove that it equals \(2\).

Finally, if \(n\) is prime, its only positive divisors are \(1\) and \(n\), so \(\ell(n)=n\). Substitution into the exact formulas yields
\[
\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)=2n,
\]
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(4)-\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)
=2(n-1)^2+2-2n
=2(n-1)(n-2),
\]
and
\[
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}
=n\left(1-\frac2n+\frac{2}{n^2}\right)
=n-2+\frac2n.
\]
This is the claimed prime-size linear-scale ratio separation.
